title: Pork Bacon, Smoked or Cured, Cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Pork bacon is a pre‑processed pork product that is smoked or cured and then cooked. It is made from the pork belly, which is salted, sometimes sweetened and spiced, and then smoked over wood. The finished product has a distinctive aroma, firm texture, and rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bacon was known in ancient Rome, where it was called "petaso".
Smoking not only adds flavor but also extends the product’s shelf life.
In the United States bacon is often served as crisp strips, while in Europe it is commonly used in chunks for dishes.
There are several types: smoked, cured, and pre‑cooked (ready to eat).
A traditional English breakfast typically includes bacon, eggs, beans, and tomatoes.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Bacon provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Choline
items.content: Choline supports liver health and nervous system function.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: Rich in protein and fat, bacon can help maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: The curing salt makes bacon high in sodium, which can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Bacon contains a large proportion of saturated fat, which may affect cholesterol levels when consumed in excess.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: These are often added for preservation and color; high intake may lead to formation of potentially harmful compounds.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: A small number of people may have allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bacon is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bacon can be pan‑fried until crisp, baked in the oven, or added to soups, salads, pasta, and omelets. It is also used as a flavor base for sauces and stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bacon in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 7‑10 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration, which indicate spoilage.
